S.title: Cerebral cavernous malformations: epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, diagnosis and therapy.
S.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are cerebrovascular diseases characterized by vascular lesions of the central nervous system (CNS) that can result in epileptic seizures, headaches, focal neurologic deficits (FNDs), and hemorrhagic stroke. Germline and somatic loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in one of the three established CCM-associated genes, namely CCM1 (or krev interaction trapped protein 1, KRIT1), CCM2, and CCM3 (or programmed cell death 10, PDCD10), which have been validated as core drivers of CCM pathogenesis and progression. Over the past few decades, a substantially improved understanding of the hallmarks and molecular basis of CCMs has been achieved. Key pathological hallmarks include but are not limited to excessive angiogenesis, vascular leakage, endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), defective autophagy, inflammation and immune response, oxidative stress, influenced gut microbiome and altered brain vascular microenvironment. These hallmarks are orchestrated by dysregulated signaling cascades, notably MEKK3-KLF2/4, PI3K-mTOR, and RhoA-ROCK, which integrate genetic, inflammatory, and hemodynamic cues. Concurrently, sophisticated neuroimaging (MRI with SWI/QSM) and genetic testing now enable precise diagnosis and risk stratification. Although surgical resection remains the mainstay for accessible symptomatic lesions, a wave of mechanism‑based pharmacological candidates has shown promising efficacy in preclinical models, and several have advanced to early‑phase clinical trials. This review summarizes the current understanding of CCM epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, diagnosis and therapy, highlighting how the evolving multi‑hit concept and the dissection of downstream signaling are paving the way towards personalized management of this complicated vascular disease.

A.title: Basic research and surgical techniques for brain arteriovenous malformations.
A.abstract: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are hemorrhagic vascular diseases in which arteries and veins are directly connected with no capillary bed between the two. We herein introduce the results of basic research of this disease and surgical techniques based on our data and experiences. The results obtained from our research show that cell death- and inflammation-related molecules changed or became activated compared with control specimens. These findings indicate that chronic inflammation occurs in and around the nidus of AVMs. Various molecules are involved in the mechanisms of cell death and angiogenesis during this process. Confirmation of blood flow in the nidus is very important to avoid hemorrhagic complications during surgical removal of the nidus. The risk of hemorrhage increases when the blood flow in the nidus is not reduced. We reported the advantages of serial indocyanine green videoangiography, which is used to assess the blood flow during AVM nidus removal. Since publication of the ARUBA trial and Scottish Audit, treatments with high morbidity have not been allowed. It is especially important for neurosurgeons to treat low Spetzler-Martin grade AVMs with low morbidity. J. Med. Invest. 67 : 222-228, August, 2020.

A.title: Effectiveness of LDL Apheresis Techniques for Reducing LDL-C in Familial Hypercholesterolemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
A.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a common inherited disorder characterized by markedly elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and an increased risk of premature cardiovascular disease. LDL apheresis is an extracorporeal procedure used to remove atherogenic lipoproteins from the circulation and is an established treatment option for selected patients with FH. This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze the effectiveness of different LDL apheresis techniques in reducing LDL-C and other lipid parameters in patients with FH.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted on 9 March, 2025. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, EMBASE, and Google Scholar were searched using relevant keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, without restrictions on publication date or publication status. Data were extracted and managed using EndNote and Microsoft Excel, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 2017. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklists. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore potential differences according to study characteristics. Random-effects models were used to account for between-study heterogeneity.
RESULTS: Of 1060 records identified through database and reference-list searches, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria. Germany contributed the largest number of included studies (n = 21). The pooled mean values following LDL apheresis were 163.40 mg/dL for total cholesterol (TC; 95% CI, 135.47-191.34; I 2 = 98.47%), 122.99 mg/dL for LDL-C (95% CI, 105.46-140.51; I 2 = 96.71%), 19.41 mg/dL for lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] (95% CI, 9.84-28.98; I 2 = 96.83%), and 7.06 mg/dL for high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) (95% CI, 5.24-8.89; I 2 = 80.87%). The pooled reduction in triglycerides (TG) was 46.94 mg/dL (95% CI, 32.88-60.99; I 2 = 98.47%). Among the evaluated techniques, double-filtration plasmapheresis (DFPP) showed the greatest reductions in TC, LDL-C, and HDL-C, with pooled reductions of 354.42, 281.82, and 15.75 mg/dL, respectively. No statistically significant differences among LDL apheresis techniques were observed for reductions in TG or Lp(a). Overall, the available evidence indicated reductions in these lipid parameters across the evaluated techniques, although substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed.
CONCLUSION: LDL apheresis was associated with substantial reductions in TC, LDL-C, HDL-C, TG, and Lp(a) in patients with FH. The available evidence suggests that different LDL apheresis techniques have broadly comparable effects on TG and Lp(a), whereas DFPP demonstrated greater reductions in TC, LDL-C, and HDL-C in the available comparative evidence. However, the safety evidence should be interpreted cautiously because adverse events were not quantitatively synthesized and reporting varied across studies. Therefore, the available evidence does not permit definitive conclusions regarding the comparative safety of LDL apheresis techniques. In clinical practice, selection of a specific technique should consider treatment characteristics, patient tolerance, technical requirements, resource availability, and cost considerations in addition to lipid-lowering efficacy.

A.title: Re-treatment of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) in the post-SID-GBS trial era.
A.abstract:
INTRODUCTION/AIMS: Combining plasma exchange (PE) and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or sequential treatment courses in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) has not been shown to provide additional benefit over single-course treatment. However, the extent to which re-treatment persists in clinical practice remains unknown. In this study, we aimed to determine the frequency of retreatment, identify factors associated with re-treatment, and compare outcomes between single-treatment and retreated patients.
METHODS: All patients who underwent inpatient electromyography and nerve conduction studies (EMG/NCS) at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania between July 1, 2019 and May 30, 2025 were screened to identify those diagnosed with GBS. Demographics, treatment details, and outcome (defined by GBS disability score [GBS-DS]) were extracted from clinical records and compared between patients receiving single treatment versus retreatment using t-tests for continuous variables and Fisher's exact tests for categorical variables.
RESULTS: Sixty-eight GBS patients were included. Ten patients who did not improve within 1 week after their first treatment were re-treated. There were no significant predisposing factors for re-treatment. Outcome at 6 months was similar between those who were re-treated versus those who were not. Most re-treated patients received more than one round of re-treatment. The most common reasons for re-treatment included clinical worsening or plateau and patient perception of returning symptoms.
DISCUSSION: A substantial minority of GBS patients continued to receive re-treatment at this single academic medical center despite lack of supporting evidence. The absence of clear clinical variables associated with retreatment suggests that non-evidence-based factors may influence these decisions.

A.title: Case Report: Recurrence of recipient-derived erythropoiesis in hematopoietic stem cell transplant for sickle-cell anemia: multi-lineage chimerism analysis as a tool to distinguish atypical pure red cell aplasia from poor erythroid engraftment.
A.abstract: Experience in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) as a long-term curative treatment for sickle-cell anemia (SCA) has been gathered over the last 30 years. Sustained engraftment to restore normal erythropoiesis remains the primary aim of HSCT in this disease. Yet, with the increasing use of reduced intensity conditioning as a toxicity-sparing alternative, a significant proportion of transplanted patients develop mixed chimerism. While a myeloid donor chimerism above 20% is deemed sufficient to prevent pain crisis, patients with donor chimerism below 50% can present recurrence of hemolytic features (1). Although experimental studies have demonstrated the feasibility of chimerism analysis on CD71-positive erythroblasts as well as earlier erythroid precursors such as BFU-E and CFU-GM, their clinical benefit remains debated (2, 3). Herein we report the unusual case of a 15 year-old patient transplanted for SCA who developed Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA), followed by the recurrence of hemolytic anemia and rising HbS levels upon reticulocyte recovery. The patient failed to respond to standard treatment with Rituximab and Daratumumab for PRCA, which further raised concern for poor donor erythroid engraftment or secondary graft failure. In this setting, the information supplied by lineage-specific chimerism, particularly B-cell and erythroid progenitor chimerism, which were both predominantly of donor origin, helped distinguishing the two conditions and guide clinical decision-making. The hematological condition of the patient dramatically improved upon donor-derived B-cell recovery and initiation of plasmapheresis. This clinical report makes an argument for lineage-specific chimerism in patients with hemoglobinopathies experiencing recurrence of hemolytic anemia after PRCA.

A.title: Olezarsen and Beyond: Emerging Targeted Treatments for Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome and Related Triglyceride Disorders.
A.abstract: In familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), a rare lipid disorder, triglycerides rise to extremely high levels because of the inability to utilize lipoprotein lipase (LPL) for fat metabolism. Traditional triglyceride-lowering medications are ineffective, leaving patients dependent on strict low-fat diets. This review examines emerging non-LPL-based therapies for FCS. This narrative review assessed therapeutic strategies targeting key regulators of triglyceride metabolism, including apolipoprotein C-III (APOC3) and angiopoietin-like protein 3 (ANGPTL3), in both animal and human studies. Investigational approaches included monoclonal antibodies, RNA-based therapies, gene therapy modalities, genome editing platforms, and plasmapheresis. Olezarsen effectively lowers triglycerides with greater safety than older options. Other agents, such as ANGPTL3 inhibitors and RNA interference therapies, also reduce lipids and provide additional treatment options. Gene therapy and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 approaches are expected to become available in the near future, while plasmapheresis remains an intervention for acute pancreatitis. Innovative therapies targeting APOC3, ANGPTL3, or liver-specific genes are transforming the management of FCS. These advances not only address this rare disorder but also offer insights into treating triglyceride-related cardiovascular risk and lipid abnormalities. Although some uncertainties remain, the outlook for FCS therapy appears highly promising.

A.title: [Immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura successfully diagnosed and treated through repeated ADAMTS13 inhibitor testing].
A.abstract: Immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is characterized by systemic thrombosis and organ damage due to a significant reduction in ADAMTS13 enzyme activity caused by the production of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies. The standard frontline treatments are supplementation of ADAMTS13 and the removal of inhibitory antibodies by plasma exchange, suppression of inhibitor generation by corticosteroid, and suppression of thrombosis formation by caplacizumab. Additionally, in recurrent or refractory cases, favorable outcomes have been reported using rituximab. It has been reported that low ADAMTS13 inhibitor titers result in false negatives, and these rise to detectable levels due to a reaction to the ADAMTS13 factor in the fresh frozen plasma used in plasma exchange. Here, we report a case where the ADAMTS13 activity was <10%, but the ADAMTS13 inhibitor was negative at the initial measurement. It is difficult to distinguish between congenital and immune-mediated TTP. We experienced a rare case in which the patient's life was saved by continuing treatment for immune-mediated TTP while conducting a thorough examination of differential diagnoses. This rare case is presented together with a review of the relevant literature.

A.title: A GLP-1/apelin dual receptor agonist shows neuroprotective effects in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
A.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) class of drugs is on the market to treat diabetes and obesity. GLP-1 drugs have also shown neuroprotective effects in animal models and clinical trials in PD patients. Apelin (APJ) is an adipokine peptide hormone with neuroprotective actions in preclinical studies. Here, we test the effects of a rationally designed bifunctional peptide, namely ELA (exendin-4-linker-apelin), in the MPTP mouse model of PD. The single GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide was used as a comparator. Motor activity was improved by both drugs (open field, pole test, Rotarod), and the inflammation response was reduced (activation of microglia and astrocytes, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels). In addition, synapse numbers were improved in the striatum (Golgi strain, TEM), expression of synapse-associated proteins was enhanced, alongside reduced expression of genes that increase mitochondrial fission. Mitochondrial fusion gene expressions (Opa1, Mfn2, Drp1) and mitochondrial morphology were also normalized (TEM). ELA was superior to liraglutide in some, but not all, parameters measured. The results suggest that the rational design of bifunctional peptides targeting both GLP-1 and APJ pathways-with optimized pharmacokinetics and enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability-merits further investigation as a strategy for developing more effective treatments for PD.

A.title: Microbiota-regulated TCDCA associates with Parkinson's disease severity and promotes BBB dysfunction through VSMC TGR5 signaling in mice.
A.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a systemic disorder linked to gut dysbiosis, yet key microbiota-regulated metabolites remain unclear. Here, we observe elevated taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) in patients with PD that correlates with disease severity. Reduced bile salt hydrolase (BSH) gene abundance correlates inversely with circulating TCDCA, consistent with altered bile acid deconjugation. Exogenous TCDCA correlates with aggravated motor and gastrointestinal deficits, impaired blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and accelerated dopaminergic neurodegeneration in a PD mouse model. Mechanistically, TCDCA links to TGR5 signaling activation in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), alongside PKCα-dependent mitochondrial apoptosis and BBB disruption. VSMC-specific Tgr5 deletion coincides with neurovascular protection. Supplementation with a BSH-high Lactobacillus reuteri strain reduces TCDCA concentrations, improves gut and BBB integrity, mitigates inflammation, and alleviates PD-like phenotypes in a BSH-dependent manner. These data support a gut-BBB-brain axis linked to PD, identifying TCDCA as a candidate pathological marker.

A.title: Effective treatment of gastrointestinal bleeding with thalidomide--Chances and limitations.
A.abstract: For more than 50 years bleeding from gastrointestinal angiodysplasias has been treated by hormonal therapy with estrogens and progesterons. After a randomized study finally demonstrated that hormones have no effect on bleeding events and transfusion requirements, therapy has switched to endoscopic coagulation. However, angiodysplasias tend to recur over months to years and endoscopy often has to be repeated for long time periods. Thalidomide, which caused severe deformities in newborn children in the 1960s, is now increasingly used after it was shown to suppress tumor necrosis factor alpha, inhibit angiogenesis and to be also effective for treatment of multiple myeloma. In 2011 thalidomide was proven to be highly effective for treatment of bleeding from gastrointestinal angiodysplasias in a randomized study. Further evidence by uncontrolled studies exists that thalidomide is also useful for treatment of bleeding in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. In spite of this data, endoscopic therapy remains the treatment of choice in many hospitals, as thalidomide is still notorious for its teratogenicity. However, patients with gastrointestinal bleeding related to angiodysplasias are generally at an age in which women have no child-bearing potential. Teratogenicity is therefore no issue for these elderly patients. Other side-effects of thalidomide like neurotoxicity may limit treatment options but can be monitored safely.

A.title: Epileptogenesis in neurocutaneous disorders with focus in Sturge Weber syndrome.
A.abstract: Epilepsy is a major morbidity in Sturge Weber syndrome, a segmental vascular neurocutaneous disorder classically associated with facial angiomas, glaucoma, and leptomeningeal capillary-venous type vascular malformations. The extent of the latter correlates with neurological outcome. Post-zygotic mosaicism for the activating mutation p.R183Q of the GNAQ gene has been identified as the major cause. GNAQ encodes for an alpha subunit of a heterotrimeric G protein critical to blood vessel development. The earlier the timing of the mutation in development, the more severe the involvement, e.g. from isolated port-wine stains to the full syndrome. The strongest predictors of adverse outcomes are MRI and the presence of angiomas involving any part of the forehead, delineated inferiorly from the outer canthus of the eye to the top of the ear, and including the upper eyelid. The neurological course may be progressive and the typical constellation of symptoms is focal onset seizures, hemiparesis, headache, stroke-like episodes, behavior problems, intellectual disability, and visual field deficits. Antiseizure medications are effective in about half of patients. The presence of localized seizures, focal neurological deficits, and drug resistant epilepsy indicate epilepsy surgical evaluation. Earlier seizure onset, i.e. before six months of age, is associated with a more severe course with significant residual deficits. Factors contributing to epileptogenesis include decreased brain tissue perfusion due to abnormal venous drainage, anoxic injury contributing to cerebral calcification, breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, and the presence of developmental cortical malformations. Pre-symptomatic prophylactic treatment may be a future option to modify the course of the disease including the associated epileptogenesis.

A.title: RNA-Sequencing Highlights Inflammation and Impaired Integrity of the Vascular Wall in Brain Arteriovenous Malformations.
A.abstract: Background and Purpose- Interventional treatment of unruptured brain arteriovenous malformations (BAVMs) has become increasingly controversial. Because medical therapy is still lacking, we aimed to obtain insight into the disease mechanisms implicated in BAVMs and to identify potential targets for medical treatment to prevent rupture of a BAVM. Methods- We used next-generation RNA sequencing to identify differential expression on a transcriptome-wide level comparing tissue samples of 12 BAVMs to 16 intracranial control arteries. We identified differentially expressed genes by negative binominal generalized log-linear regression (false discovery rate corrected P<0.05). We selected 10 genes for validation using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction. We performed functional pathway analysis accounting for potential gene-length bias, to establish enhancement of biological pathways involved in BAVMs. We further assessed which Gene Ontology terms were enriched. Results- We found 736 upregulated genes in BAVMs including genes implicated in the cytoskeletal machinery and cell-migration and genes encoding for inflammatory cytokines and secretory products of neutrophils and macrophages. Furthermore, we found 498 genes downregulated including genes implicated in extracellular matrix composition, the binary angiopoietin-TIE system, and TGF (transforming growth factor)-β signaling. We confirmed the differential expression of top 10 ranked genes. Functional pathway analysis showed enrichment of the protein digestion and absorption pathway (false discovery rate-adjusted P=1.70×10-2). We identified 47 enriched Gene Ontology terms (false discovery rate-adjusted P<0.05) implicated in cytoskeleton network, cell-migration, endoplasmic reticulum, transmembrane transport, and extracellular matrix composition. Conclusions- Our genome-wide RNA-sequencing study points to involvement of inflammatory mediators, loss of cerebrovascular quiescence, and impaired integrity of the vascular wall in the pathophysiology of BAVMs. Our study may lend support to potential receptivity of BAVMs to medical therapeutics, including those promoting vessel maturation, and anti-inflammatory and immune-modifying drugs.

A.title: Propranolol vs prednisolone for symptomatic proliferating infantile hemangiomas: a randomized clinical trial.
A.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: While propranolol is touted as superior to prednisolone for treating infantile hemangiomas (IH), a randomized clinical trial (RCT) comparing the outcome and tolerability of these medications for symptomatic, proliferating IH has not been reported.
OBJECTIVES: To determine if oral propranolol is more efficacious and better tolerated than prednisolone in treating symptomatic, proliferating IH and to determine the feasibility of conducting a multi-institutional, RCT comparing efficacy and tolerability of both medications.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Phase 2, investigator-blinded, multi-institutional RCT conducted in 3 academic vascular anomalies clinics on 19 of 44 eligible infants aged between 2 weeks and 6 months. All participating patients had symptomatic proliferating IH treated between September 1, 2010, and August 1, 2012.
INTERVENTIONS: Treatment with oral propranolol vs prednisolone (2.0 mg/kg/d) until halted owing to toxic effects or clinical response.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcome was change in IH size after 4 months of therapy. Secondary outcomes were response rate and frequency and severity of adverse events (AEs).
RESULTS: The primary outcome showed no difference in lesion size or affected skin area after 4 months of therapy: 41% and 1.32 mm2 for prednisolone vs 64% and 0.55 mm2 for propranolol (P = .12 for lesion size, and P = .56 for affected skin area). Longitudinal analyses showed a faster response in total lesion outer dimension with prednisolone (P = .03), but this advantage over time was not noted when central clearing and outer dimension were included in the analysis (P = .91). The overall frequency of AEs was similar (44 for prednisolone vs 32 for propranolol) (P = .84), but prednisolone-treated participants had more grade 3 severe AEs (11 vs 1) (P = .01), particularly growth retardation resulting in size and weight below the fifth percentile. Early study withdrawal owing to AEs occurred in 6 (75%) of 8 patients in the prednisolone group but 0 of 11 propranolol-treated participants. The mean duration of therapy was shorter for prednisolone (141 vs 265 days), reflecting the higher rate of early withdrawals.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Both medications show similar efficacy for reducing the area of symptomatic, proliferating IH. Although prednisolone showed a faster response rate, propranolol was better tolerated with significantly fewer severe AEs. Propranolol should be the first line of therapy for symptomatic IH unless contraindicated or unless future studies demonstrate severe AEs from propranolol. Recruiting participants for a phase 3 RCT would be difficult owing to safety profiles measured here and emerging trends favoring propranolol. A.title: [Extracranial vascular anomalies (hemangiomas and vascular malformations) in children and adolescents--diagnosis, clinic, and therapy].
A.abstract: The field of extracranial vascular anomalies is considered as special focus of pediatric otolaryngology and it has shown a rapid development during the last years. The reason for this interest is finally also due to the global acceptance of the classification introduced by the ISSVA (International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies). Hemangiomas are the most frequently observed vascular tumors. Today the systemic propranolol therapy is mostly used for therapy of hemangiomas requiring treatment. Increasingly, the topical application of beta blocker is discussed while the benefit in the head and neck seems to be limited. Vascular malformations are classified according to the morphology of the affected part of the vascular system in arterial, venous, arterio-venous, lymphatic, capillary, and combined vascular malformations. Conventional surgery, sclerosing therapy, and laser treatment are invasive options for the treatment of lymphatic malformations. The options for the treatment of venous malformations could be significantly improved during the last years. In this context, the use of Nd:YAG laser, the conservative treatment of the localized disseminated intravascular coagulation with low-molecular weight heparin, the re-discovery of bleomycin as effective sclerosing agent, and the improvement of alcohol-based embolization agents must be mentioned. Today the treatment with dye laser is the preferred therapy for capillary malformations and it is superior to other therapeutic options as for example photodynamic therapy. Arterio-venous malformations as representatives for high-flow lesions are the high-risk lesions. Frequently they are compared to malignant head and neck tumors, in particular when a curative treatment can no longer be assured because of diffuse or multifocal extent and when the disease shows a progressive course. The combined treatment of embolization and surgical resection and if necessary consecutive defect reconstruction have turned out to be appropriate for arterio-venous malformations. Incurable findings are still a major challenge. Despite the introduction of antiangiogenetic drugs in oncology, the medicamentous therapeutic approach could not be established for arterio-venous malformations up to now.

A.title: Genetics of lymphatic anomalies.
A.abstract: Lymphatic anomalies include a variety of developmental and/or functional defects affecting the lymphatic vessels: sporadic and familial forms of primary lymphedema, secondary lymphedema, chylothorax and chylous ascites, lymphatic malformations, and overgrowth syndromes with a lymphatic component. Germline mutations have been identified in at least 20 genes that encode proteins acting around VEGFR-3 signaling but also downstream of other tyrosine kinase receptors. These mutations exert their effects via the RAS/MAPK and the PI3K/AKT pathways and explain more than a quarter of the incidence of primary lymphedema, mostly of inherited forms. More common forms may also result from multigenic effects or post-zygotic mutations. Most of the corresponding murine knockouts are homozygous lethal, while heterozygotes are healthy, which suggests differences in human and murine physiology and the influence of other factors.

A.title: Nursing Protocols and Observed Outcomes of TR-350 Immunoadsorption in Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder: A Single-Center Experience of 334 Procedures.
A.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We describe an institutional nursing protocol used for patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) undergoing TR-350 tryptophan immunoadsorption (IA) therapy. We retrospectively analyzed the clinical and nursing records of 67 patients with NMOSD who underwent TR-350 IA between January 2019 and August 2025.
METHODS: We evaluated 334 treatment sessions and recorded demographic characteristics, observed clinical and serological changes, adverse events, and device alarms. Nursing management before, during, and after the procedure was reviewed.
RESULTS: After the IA treatment course, reductions in the median Expanded Disability Status Scale score and the geometric mean anti-aquaporin-4 immunoglobulin G (AQP4-IgG) titer, together with improvement in visual acuity, were observed. Laboratory testing revealed hypofibrinogenemia (<1.0 g/L) in 13 of 67 patients (19.4%). Nurses identified hypotension in two sessions (2/334, 0.6%) and catheter-site bleeding in one session (1/334, 0.3%); in all, 29 device-alarm events were recorded. With nursing intervention and timely troubleshooting, 333 of 334 sessions were completed; one session (0.3%) was terminated prematurely because of extracorporeal circuit clotting.
CONCLUSION: TR-350 IA demonstrated feasibility and safety in this cohort of patients with steroid-refractory NMOSD. Adherence to nursing protocols refined locally from institutional standard operating procedures and clinical experience, together with proactive management of complications, supported a high treatment completion rate and patient safety.

A.title: Successful Use of Sutimlimab in two Pediatric Patients With Refractory Cold Antibody-Mediated Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia.
A.abstract: Cold antibody-mediated autoimmune hemolytic anemia, or cold agglutinin syndrome (CAS), in pediatrics is typically transient, although it can often be severe and require transfusion support. Recurrence in children is rare, but those with underlying immune dysfunction can have a refractory course with limited options available. We report a 4-year-old girl with Evans syndrome and life-threatening CAS refractory to transfusions, plasmapheresis, steroids, and immunosuppression as well as a 12-month-old boy status post liver transplant with CAS refractory to steroids, rituximab, and tacrolimus cessation with transition to sirolimus, both of whom received sutimlimab, a C1s inhibitor, with rapid improvement in hemolysis, transfusion independence, and a sustained remission. To our knowledge, these are the first reported uses of sutimlimab in the pediatric population.

A.title: Biphasic hypertriglyceridemia in pregnancy with apolipoprotein C-II deficiency.
A.abstract: Apolipoprotein C-II (ApoC-II) deficiency is a rare genetic cause of familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS) that predisposes affected individuals to severe hypertriglyceridemia and acute pancreatitis. Evidence guiding management during pregnancy is limited. We report a woman with ApoC-II deficiency (ApoC-II Wakayama mutation) who showed a biphasic triglyceride (TG) elevation. TG increased markedly in the second trimester, improved with intensified dietary restriction, and rose again to 1400 mg/dL (15.8 mmol/L) in the third trimester. Because she remained asymptomatic and TG had responded to dietary therapy, medical therapy and plasma exchange were not initiated. Labour was induced at 36 weeks, resulting in uncomplicated vaginal delivery and rapid postpartum TG reduction. This case highlights trimester-specific monitoring and individualized reassessment of dietary, medical, plasma exchange, and delivery strategies in FCS.

A.title: A Single Center Retrospective Study: Efficacy and Platelet Preservation of Double Plasma Molecular Adsorption System Therapy by Membrane Separation Versus Centrifugal Separation in Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure Patients With Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
A.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and liver failure. The double plasma molecular adsorption system (DPMAS) reduces bilirubin and may create a therapeutic window for anti-tumor therapy in HCC patients. Two plasma separation techniques are used: membrane-based (MBS-DPMAS) and centrifugal (CPS-DPMAS), but no study has compared them specifically in HCC patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF). This retrospective study included 203 HBV-related HCC patients who received DPMAS without plasma exchange (93 MBS-DPMAS, 110 CPS-DPMAS), with citrate anticoagulation used in all cases. Bilirubin, liver enzymes, INR, and platelet count were compared between groups and before versus after treatment. Baseline characteristics were comparable. CPS-DPMAS showed superior bilirubin reduction (TBIL: 184.60 vs. 220.05 μmol/L, p = 0.002; DBIL: 156.04 vs. 183.55 μmol/L, p = 0.004), whereas platelet count was significantly higher after MBS-DPMAS than after CPS-DPMAS (135.35 vs. 106.32 × 109/L, p = 0.012). Both modalities decreased INR transiently, and only MBS-DPMAS significantly reduced ALT, AST, and creatinine. In conclusion, both techniques effectively reduce bilirubin and decrease INR, but CPS-DPMAS offers better bilirubin clearance while MBS-DPMAS provides better platelet protection, suggesting that technique selection should be individualized.

A.title: A Rapidly Progressive Case of Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever in Pregnancy Presenting with HELLP-Like Features and Resulting in Maternal and Fetal Death.
A.abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a life-threatening viral infection that may mimic hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome during pregnancy. We describe a 30-year-old woman at 23 weeks' gestation who presented with fever, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, and severe transaminase elevation. Initial suspicion of HELLP syndrome was reconsidered in the presence of high fever, rural exposure, and rapidly progressive coagulopathy. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction. Despite intensive supportive therapy and plasmapheresis, fulminant multiorgan failure developed, resulting in maternal and fetal death. This case underscores the need to consider CCHF in febrile pregnant patients with thrombocytopenia in endemic areas.

A.title: Targeting ROCK Isoforms by Natural Phytocompounds: An In-Silico Approach to Modulate Mitochondrial Fission and Mitophagy in Neurological Diseases.
A.abstract: One of the major key organelles for neuronal survival is the mitochondria. To maintain synaptic functions and neurotransmission, these cells rely upon high ATP levels and the regulated process of mitochondrial dynamics (fission and fusion) and mitophagy. Dysregulation in any of the mitochondrial processes, such as excessive fission and/or impaired removal of damaged mitochondria, can lead to damage to nerve cells and cause neuroinflammation, a major cause of various neurodegenerative diseases. Rho-associated coiled-coil kinase isoforms (ROCK1 and ROCK2) have emerged as critical upstream regulators of mitochondrial dynamics, where ROCK1 promotes Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission. On the other hand, ROCK2 suppresses PINK1-Parkin-dependent mitophagy. Overexpression of both ROCK isoforms leads to increased ROS production and reduced ATP generation, compromising neuronal health. Although synthetic ROCK inhibitors show neuroprotective potential, their long-term clinical use is limited due to their toxicity, poor pharmacokinetics, and suboptimal BBB penetration. In contrast, natural compounds may offer a safer, cheaper and more effective inhibitory effect. The current study follows an integrated in-silico approach to screen natural phytochemicals derived from Indian medicinal plants, known for their neuroprotective effects. Based on neuroprotective properties and less explored mechanistic potential,11 plants were selected. From these plants, a library of 1,223 natural product compounds was downloaded, and a further 428 unique phytocompounds were obtained after curation with the known inhibitor for reference. These compounds were screened against key proteins ROCK1 and ROCK2 using molecular docking, followed by pharmacokinetic and toxicity class, MM-GBSA free binding energy, and molecular dynamics simulations for 200 ns. Several natural phytocompounds showed comparable binding affinities with respect to known inhibitors. Based on all the in-silico observations, Scopolin and Lycorine emerged as promising ROCK1 inhibitors, while Cytisoside and N-Methyltyramine demonstrated strong ROCK2 inhibition. Notably, Coumarin exhibited stable and persistent interactions with both ROCK1 and ROCK2, with good binding energies, high blood-brain barrier permeability, and strong dynamic stability across simulations. Collectively, all these findings indicate the natural phytochemicals as viable modulators of mitochondrial quality control. Particularly, Coumarin emerges as a promising dual ROCK inhibitor; its potential to restore mitochondrial fission and mitophagy balance and mitigate neurodegenerative diseases may be further validated using in vitro assays.

A.title: Oxidized mitochondrial DNA as a potential biomarker and mechanistic driver of autophagy-mitophagy dysregulation in pulmonary arterial hypertension: a narrative review.
A.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is recognized as a mitochondria-centered disease characterized by early bioenergetic and redox abnormalities that influence pulmonary vascular remodeling. Oxidized mitochondrial DNA (Ox-mtDNA), which combines mitochondrial stress with innate immune activation and dysregulated Ca2+ signaling to sustain hyperproliferation and apoptosis resistance in pulmonary arterial endothelial and smooth muscle cells, is a persistent danger signal rather than just a result of mitochondrial injury. Vasodilator therapy targeting the prostacyclin, nitric oxide, and endothelin pathways has made great strides, yet many patients still make progress. These treatments primarily enhance hemodynamics and vasomotor tone, but they do not directly reverse the cellular and molecular mechanisms that sustain pulmonary vascular remodeling. In this model, inflammatory signaling and mitochondrial redox imbalance are mutually reinforcing rather than strictly sequential: oxidative stress produces Ox-mtDNA, which mediates inflammatory activation, and cytokine and interferon signaling from the inflammatory process further weakens antioxidant defenses and mitochondrial respiration, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) output. Because Ox-mtDNA's synthesis, escape, sensing, and clearance all influence inflammatory tone and Ca2+ homeostasis, convergent experimental and clinical observations support Ox-mtDNA as an upstream, therapeutically actionable node. This review describes how mtDNA oxidation, reactive oxygen species amplification, and mitochondrial Ca2+ overload are all facilitated by the convergence of chronic hypoxia, inflammatory cytokines, altered shear stress, and genetic vulnerability. According to the literature, oxidative lesions increase mtDNA bioactivity and persistence when nuclease and autophagy-lysosome clearance systems are overloaded. Pathways of cytosolic and extracellular mtDNA escape, such as vesicular export, mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) or voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC)-dependent leakage, and sublethal membrane permeabilization, are summarized in this review. It is also explained how Ox-mtDNA rewires the autophagy-mitophagy axis through reduced flux and skewed signaling, allowing injured mitochondria to continue acting as signal emitters. ER Ca2+ handling and stress-induced remodeling of ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs) as upstream amplifiers of mitochondrial damage are also covered. Instead of using prospective, longitudinal cohorts, the majority of these mechanistic data and the correlation between circulating Ox-mtDNA and PAH severity are now based on cross-sectional human sampling and non-PAH disease models. Therefore, until such validation is completed, the biomarker potential of Ox-mtDNA should be considered hypothesis-generating.

A.title: Low-Density Lipoprotein Receptor-Targeted Biomimetic Nanoplatform Suppresses Glioblastoma Stemness and Remodels Antitumor Immunity via Dual Metabolic Disruption.
A.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most lethal malignancies because durable tumor control is constrained by limited brain-tumor drug exposure, metabolic plasticity, stem-like tumor states, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. We developed apolipoprotein B fragment-decorated nanoparticles co-loaded with regorafenib and erythrodiol (ApoBf-R/E@NPs), a low-density lipoprotein receptor-oriented biomimetic nanoplatform that couples brain-tumor delivery with coordinated dual-drug exposure. Fixed-ratio combination-index analysis demonstrated synergy between the two agents. Regorafenib disrupts autophagy-associated nutrient salvage and restricts angiogenic support, whereas erythrodiol stabilizes ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 and depletes cellular cholesterol. These complementary perturbations converge on ATP depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and suppression of phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B and mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling. Across established and patient-derived GBM models, treatment broadly impaired tumor-cell survival while suppressing stemness-associated programs and reducing viability and tumorsphere persistence in patient-derived glioma stem-like cell cultures. Treatment also promoted an immunogenic cell death-associated tumor-cell state and antitumor immune remodeling. In immunocompetent GBM models, ApoBf-R/E@NPs showed preferential intracranial tumor-associated delivery, suppressed orthotopic and untreated distal tumor growth, and delayed postoperative regrowth, accompanied by systemic immune remodeling and expansion of memory-associated T-cell populations. These findings establish a blood-brain barrier-oriented nanodelivery strategy that couples complementary metabolic vulnerabilities to broad GBM control, stem-like compartment suppression, and antitumor immunity.

A.title: An icariin-loaded Polycaprolactone (PCL) electrospun scaffold for enhanced tendon-bone healing in rotator cuff repair.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to fabricate an icariin (ICA)-loaded polycaprolactone (PCL) electrospun scaffold and systematically evaluate its effects on tendon-bone healing in a rat rotator cuff injury model, with particular focus on its immunomodulatory, angiogenic, and fibrocartilaginous regeneration capabilities.
METHODS: ICA-PCL scaffolds were prepared using electrospinning technology and characterized for microstructure, drug release kinetics, and cytocompatibility. In vitro experiments involved lipopolysaccharide-induced rat bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells and brain microvascular endothelial cells to assess anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and proangiogenic effects. In vivo evaluations were conducted in a rat rotator cuff injury model using histological staining, immunofluorescence, western blot, and Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay to analyze tissue regeneration, macrophage polarization, and safety profiles at 4 and 8 weeks postimplantation.
RESULTS: The ICA-PCL scaffold displayed a biphasic release pattern with initial burst release followed by sustained ICA delivery. In vitro, it significantly enhanced rat bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell proliferation, reduced apoptosis and oxidative stress, downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), and promoted endothelial tube formation. In vivo results demonstrated that the scaffold modulated macrophage polarization toward M2 phenotype, enhanced angiogenesis (increased CD31/EMCN expression), and facilitated fibrocartilaginous interface regeneration with organized collagen architecture and elevated collagen I/II expression. No evident systemic toxicity or organ damage was observed.
CONCLUSION: The ICA-PCL electrospun scaffold effectively promotes tendon-bone healing through multimechanistic actions, including immunomodulation, angiogenesis promotion, and structured interface regeneration, demonstrating significant potential as a comprehensive therapeutic strategy for rotator cuff repair.

A.title: Adult-onset Coats disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis of imaging biomarkers and targeted therapies.
A.abstract: Coats disease diagnosed in adulthood is a rare idiopathic retinal telangiectatic vasculopathy that may differ in phenotype from childhood-diagnosed cases. This systematic review synthesizes current evidence to characterize its clinical spectrum, imaging features, treatment outcomes and underlying mechanisms, with a focus on immunovascular pathways. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through October 2025 for studies including patients ≥18 years with confirmed Coats disease. Clinical and imaging findings, treatment strategies and outcomes were extracted and narratively synthesized. When possible, random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Thirty-five studies comprising 240 patients (250 eyes) were included. Disease presentation was predominantly unilateral and diagnosed at Shields Stage 2 or 3. Laser photocoagulation and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents were the most frequently described therapies, with anatomical stabilization or regression of exudation reported in approximately half of treated eyes across heterogeneous studies, and better outcomes in earlier stages. Visual acuity was stabilized or improved in 57.1% of treated eyes, while recurrence occurred in 19.3%. Multimodal imaging consistently identified peripheral telangiectasia, lipid exudation and localized capillary nonperfusion. Aqueous cytokine profiling in small cohorts has reported elevated inflammatory mediators (e.g. interleukin [IL]-6 and IL-1β) in some adults, suggesting that inflammatory signalling may contribute to blood-retina barrier dysfunction and macular oedema alongside VEGF-related permeability. Current evidence supports Coats disease diagnosed in adulthood as a chronic telangiectatic retinal vasculopathy with frequent macular involvement. Therapeutic outcomes appear to favour individualized, imaging-guided combination strategies and prospective studies with standardized endpoints are needed to refine management.

A.title: ROS-autocatalytic nanoplatform interfering astrocyte-cancer crosstalk and enhancing glioblastoma therapy.
A.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains incurable and exhibits exceptionally high metabolic demands, driving the evolution of hyperactive mitochondrial systems within tumors. In parallel, mitochondrial transfer from astrocytes to cancer cells fuels metabolic reprogramming and enhances GBM tumorigenicity. These malignant traits markedly constrain therapeutic efficacy and patient survival. Herein, we report a dehydroascorbic acid (DHA)-functionalized, ROS-responsive, ferrocene-integrated polymer nanoplatform (GS@DFP) co-loaded with S-Gboxin and Galunisertib, simultaneously targeting GBM mitochondria and mitochondrial transfer in astrocyte-cancer cell crosstalk. After crossing the blood-brain barrier (BBB) through Glut1-mediated transport enabled by DHA, GS@DFP responds to elevated intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in GBM to trigger payload release and initiate Fenton reactions. S-Gboxin inhibits mitochondrial complex V and depletes ATP, whereas Galunisertib downregulates TGF-β/SMAD-driven thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) expression, suppressing tumor microtube (MT) formation and thereby reducing astrocyte-to-GBM mitochondrial transfer. Notably, TGF-β inhibition also reprograms the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). This work establishes a multifunctional nanoplatform that targets mitochondrial vulnerabilities and intercellular crosstalk, offering a translatable strategy for enhancing GBM therapy.

A.title: Coexistence of Ebstein Anomaly and Cerebral Cavernous Malformation: A Case Report.
A.abstract: In most patients who have Ebstein anomaly (EA), neurological symptoms are either associated with thromboembolic episodes or due to arrhythmic complications. Cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) is a vascular anomaly made up of sinusoidally dilated blood vessels, often presenting with seizure activity or intracranial bleeding. There has never been any documented report regarding coexisting EA and CCM. Herein, we have reported a 32-year-old female with an established history of Ebstein anomaly diagnosed in 2013 who had a history of generalized tonic-clonic fits since 2020. Neuroimaging studies showed the presence of a right frontal lobe mass with typical "popcorn-like" appearance and hemosiderin ring on MRI, indicative of cerebral cavernous malformation. The patient declined surgery and was managed conservatively with levetiracetam. With the occurrence of further fits in 2025, neuroimaging showed similar findings but without the presence of intratumoral bleeding. Subsequently, she underwent a left frontoparietal craniotomy for GTE of the lesion with cavernoma on histopathology. The neurological status of the patient was stable during her discharge on the fourth postoperative day. This case documents a previously unreported coexistence of Ebstein anomaly and cerebral cavernous malformation in a single patient. Given the rarity of both conditions, coexistence is coincidental. This indicates the need for genetic and molecular studies to determine whether a real biological association exists.

A.title: Musculoskeletal Histopathology of Klippel-Trénaunay Syndrome: A Clinicopathologic Study of 21 Cases With Long-Term Orthopedic Follow-Up.
A.abstract: Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome (KTS) is a rare congenital vascular-overgrowth disorder within the broader spectrum of PIK3CA-related overgrowth syndromes. Although clinical, radiologic, and orthopedic manifestations are well described, the histologic spectrum of KTS-associated pathology remains under-characterized. Clinicopathologic findings from 21 patients with clinically established KTS were reviewed, including 18 with longitudinal clinical follow-up and 3 consultation cases of rare malignant mesenchymal neoplasms. Cases were identified from institutional pathology and clinical databases, and available hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections and ancillary studies were reviewed. The cohort included 11 males and 10 females. Among the 18 clinically followed patients, 12 had limb length discrepancy or asymmetric limb overgrowth, 9 had documented deep vascular malformations, 4 had intra-articular/synovial malformations, and 10 underwent initial orthopedic evaluation or intervention before age 18. Orthopedic morbidity clustered into mechanical overgrowth-related, vascular malformation-related, and soft tissue/wound-related complications. Histologic findings included superficial and/or deep slow-flow vascular malformations, ulceration and granulation tissue, hemosiderin-laden reactive synovium, and destructive hemorrhagic arthropathy. Intra-articular disease recapitulated a hemophilic arthropathy-like pattern, with hemosiderotic synovitis, papillary synovial hyperplasia, and progressive joint destruction with loss of articular cartilage, exposed subchondral bone destruction and remodeling, all attributable to long-standing intra-articular hemorrhage. Three consultation cases showed malignant mesenchymal neoplasia, including 2 angiosarcomas. Recognition of these patterns is important for pathologists evaluating specimens from patients with known or suspected KTS, particularly when findings mimic hemophilic arthropathy, diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor, nonsyndromic vascular malformation, and/or end-stage destructive arthropathy.

A.title: Propranolol therapy for reducing the number of nasal infantile hemangioma invasive procedures.
A.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Propranolol therapy is changing the treatment paradigm for infantile hemangioma. This study addresses the effect of propranolol therapy on the treatment of nasal infantile hemangioma (NIH), an area that often does not respond to medical therapy.
OBJECTIVE: To determine if propranolol treatment is associated with fewer invasive treatments for NIH.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Retrospective cohort study conducted within a single pediatric institution's multidisciplinary vascular anomaly program for patients with NIH treated between January 1, 2003, and December 31, 2011. Three NIH cohorts were compared: prepropranolol (20 in group 1; 2003-2009), propranolol (25 in group 2; 2009-2011), and nonpropranolol (13 in group 3; 2009-2011) treatment.
INTERVENTIONS: Analysis of systemic medical, laser, or surgical therapies for NIH.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The study plan was created to detect a change in invasive therapy for NIH. Data collected included presenting age, sex, affected nasal subunits, infantile hemangioma morphologic characteristics, treatment type and number, and primary treating service. An NIH grading system, based on nasal subunit involvement, helped quantify treatment change. Descriptive statistics summarized data, and a Cox proportional hazards regression model evaluated propranolol use and the likelihood of invasive treatments (surgical excision or laser).
RESULTS: Of the 95 patients identified, 58 met inclusion criteria: 20 in group 1 (mean age, 4.8 months), 25 in group 2 (mean age, 4.9 months), and 13 in group 3 (mean age, 4.9 months). Nasal infantile hemangiomas involved the nasal tip subunit in 33 of 58 patients (56.9%). Eight of 13 patients (61.5%) in group 3 frequently had small NIH (grade 1). Patients in group 2 were less likely to undergo any invasive treatments (relative risk, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27-0.73), have surgical excision only (0.45; 0.15-1.38), or undergo laser treatment only (0.44; 0.27-0.78) compared with those in group 1. Patients with higher-grade NIH had more medical or invasive therapy, but invasive procedures were carried out in each subgroup defined by grade.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Patients with isolated propranolol-treated NIH were less likely to undergo invasive treatment, but despite its implementation, the need for invasive treatment was not totally supplanted by its use.

A.title: The Impact of Plasmapheresis on Serum Concentrations of Antiseizure Medications: A Systematic Review.
A.abstract: Seizures are an important neurological manifestation of several autoimmune and antibody-mediated disorders and often require treatment with antiseizure medications (ASMs). Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is frequently used to treat these antibody-mediated conditions by removing circulating pathogenic factors. However, TPE is non-selective and may also remove protein-bound ASMs, particularly those with low volume of distribution. This unintended drug clearance may result in subtherapeutic concentrations and breakthrough seizures. This study aims to systematically assess the available evidence on the effects of TPE on ASM serum concentrations. It also seeks to determine whether drug removal is clinically significant and needs post-procedure supplemental dosing. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library from April to May 2025 using predefined MeSH terms and keywords related to epilepsy, ASMs, and TPE. Randomized trials and case reports/series involving patients receiving ASMs concomitantly with TPE and reporting serum drug concentrations were included. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. The primary outcome was the effect of TPE on ASM serum concentrations and the need for dose adjustment. Eighteen studies comprising 30 patients were included. Phenytoin was the most frequently evaluated ASM; although total serum concentrations often declined during TPE, overall drug removal was generally low, and free levels frequently remained therapeutic. Phenobarbital showed minimal change, while valproate and several newer ASMs demonstrated variable reductions in serum concentrations. Breakthrough seizures were reported in seven studies, ranging from transient events to refractory seizures requiring dose adjustments or treatment discontinuation. The effect of TPE on ASM pharmacokinetics was found to be drug-specific and largely influenced by protein binding and volume of distribution. Although overall drug removal is generally limited, peri-procedural serum fluctuations may contribute to breakthrough seizures in vulnerable patients. Routine supplemental dosing is not generally recommended; instead, individualized monitoring, and post-session dosing strategies are advised, particularly for ASMs with low volume of distribution or in high-risk patients.

A.title: Case Report: Efgartigimod in refractory non-tumor Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
A.abstract: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a rare autoimmune disorder, associated with neoplastic disease in 50-60% of cases. In severe cases, currently available immunomodulatory therapies frequently fail to achieve adequate control. We report a 20-year-old woman with non-tumor LEMS refractory to 3,4-diaminopyridine, sequential immunosuppression with prednisone, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and rituximab and plasma exchange, who remained severely disabled after two years of progressive disease. Off-label efgartigimod (1000mg subcutaneously weekly for four weeks, with the interval between cycles initially adjusted according to symptom recurrence), produced rapid and sustained clinical improvement, including recovery from a respiratory decompensation episode. The Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) score decreased from a baseline of 5-9 to a minimum of 2, and the Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) score improved from 13-18 to 8-11. Symptoms consistently recurred toward the end of the third week of each treatment-free interval, prompting a fixed two-week interval, which stabilized clinical response and reduced fluctuation severity. This is, to our knowledge, the first report of sustained clinical benefit from FcRn inhibition in non-paraneoplastic, long-standing refractory LEMS. As in myasthenia gravis, LEMS is mediated by pathogenic circulating IgG antibodies, and these findings support FcRn inhibition as a rational treatment strategy in refractory LEMS regardless of tumor association.

A.title: Anti-GBM disease shortly after clinically presumed ANCA-associated vasculitis in an 85-year-old patient: a case report and literature review.
A.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Sequential emergence of anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease after anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is rare.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 85-year-old woman presented with fever, edema, elevated myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA, mild urinary abnormalities, markedly elevated urinary tubular injury markers, and negative serum anti-GBM antibodies measured by chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay. Renal biopsy was not performed because of advanced age, severe dementia, antiplatelet therapy, and the family's preference for non-invasive management. She was clinically presumed to have AAV and achieved apparent clinical remission with prednisolone alone, although MPO-ANCA remained positive. However, 2.5 months after the initial AAV diagnosis, she developed rapidly progressive kidney failure requiring dialysis, accompanied by severe hematuria, increased proteinuria, urinary casts, and markedly elevated anti-GBM antibodies. Clinically diagnosed anti-GBM disease was treated with methylprednisolone pulse therapy, prednisolone, plasma exchange, and hemodialysis. Although renal recovery was not achieved, anti-GBM antibodies became negative, and she remained clinically stable on maintenance hemodialysis for over 4 years while receiving low-dose prednisolone.
CONCLUSION: This case suggests that anti-GBM disease can emerge shortly after apparent clinical remission of AAV. ANCA-mediated GBM injury and age-related GBM changes may contribute to subsequent anti-GBM autoimmunity, although these mechanisms remain hypothetical in this patient. Prompt anti-GBM antibody testing should be considered when a rapid, unexplained decline in kidney function occurs during or after AAV treatment.

A.title: ANCA-associated vasculitis in the United Arab Emirates: a 17-year case series with review from Gulf literature.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a rare and severe autoimmune disease characterized by pauci-immune necrotizing vasculitis.
OBJECTIVES: The study aims to explore the frequency, clinical characteristics, and management of AAV patients in two tertiary centers in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) over 17 years.
DESIGN: A retrospective observational case series.
SETTING: Two tertiary centers in the UAE.
METHODS: Patients diagnosed with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) from 2008 to 2024 were included. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, histopathological information, treatment, complications, relapses, and mortality were collected. ANCA testing for anti-proteinase 3 (PR3) and anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) antibodies was performed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed to summarize the data.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Subtype distribution, organ involvement, ANCA positivity, relapse, and mortality rates.
SAMPLE SIZE: Twenty-six patients.
RESULTS: We identified 26 AAV patients with a median age of 52.5 years. The majority were females (58%, n=15), and half were locals. The most common AAV subtype was microscopic polyangiitis (50%, n=13), followed by granulomatosis with polyangiitis (38%, n=10) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (12%, n=3). ANCAs tested positive in nearly all of these cases. The most common clinical manifestations of AAV were constitutional symptoms with renal and pulmonary involvement. The induction therapy included corticosteroids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, and plasma exchange. The most prescribed maintenance medications were corticosteroids and azathioprine. The overall relapse rate was 31%, and the overall mortality rate was 19% (n=5).
CONCLUSION: In our cohort, MPA was the most common subtype, being predominantly associated with P-ANCA/MPO-ANCA positivity. Notably, few studies from the Gulf region have addressed this topic. It's unclear whether this finding reflects low occurrence or potential underdiagnosis and, thus, points to unmet needs and a significant gap in the understanding of AAV. Multicenter studies are needed to validate these results and improve AAV management in Middle Eastern populations.
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective design with small number of participants.

A.title: Immunotherapy considerations for distal sensory-predominant and small-fiber peripheral neuropathies.
A.abstract: Increasing knowledge about the common widespread, distal-predominant polyneuropathies is shifting the standard of care beyond merely palliating symptom toward intervention. This is less advanced for the more prevalent but harder-to-ascertain distal sensory polyneuropathies (DSP) than for motor and demyelinating neuropathies. DSP comprises the sensory-predominant large-fiber axonal/demyelinating neuropathies plus the small-fiber sensory/autonomic axonopathies. Small-fiber disturbances can cause premature fatigue, neuropathic pain and itch, postural orthostasis tachycardia, and gastrointestinal distress. Diagnosis is difficult - screening for classic causes is mandatory but unproductive in a third to a half of patients (initially idiopathic DSP/iiDSP). Multiple large case series and two small passive-transfer studies suggest that autoimmunity may be a prevalent cause of iiDSP, particularly for small-fiber neuropathy. So, despite the knowledge gaps, immunotherapies effective for other neuropathies are increasingly considered for dysimmune iiDSP; particularly in otherwise healthy young patients with impaired life trajectories. To inform these difficult treatment decisions, this chapter summarizes diagnostic requirements for large- and small-fiber iiDSP and evaluates the type and strength of the evidence suggesting autoimmune causality in some. Concomitant rheumatologic conditions including often undiagnosed Sjögren's syndrome, predispose. Youth, abrupt onset, other organ dysimmunity, immune seromarkers, and prior responses to immunotherapy can provide additional evidence, but autoantibody panels are almost never useful. Uncontrolled studies suggest that apparently autoimmune DSP sometimes responds to corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulins, and plasmapheresis. However, these cannot be prescribed indiscriminately due to risk, cost/availability, and lack of controlled trials and guidelines. Enough preliminary data may have accrued to permit formulating initial consensus recommendations for selecting the subsets of patients in whom immunotherapy should or should not be considered. Patients, clinicians, and payors would benefit immediately, and highlighting priorities for research could promote long-term advances.

A.title: Blood-brain barrier disruption and microglia-associated synaptic pruning contribute to cognitive decline after electroconvulsive therapy.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Modified electroconvulsive therapy (MECT) is a highly effective intervention for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its broader clinical application is constrained by poorly understood cognitive side effects. We hypothesized that MECT disrupts hippocampal blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, permitting extravasation of peripheral factors that activate microglia, drive synaptic phagocytosis, and precipitate cognitive decline.
METHODS: We employed a multi-modal translational approach integrating: (1) clinical neuroimaging (rs-fMRI and DCE-MRI) and cognitive assessments in 41 MDD patients undergoing MECT (including 9 with DCE-MRI); (2) a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model subjected to electroconvulsive shock (ECS), with behavioral, molecular, and transcriptomic analyses; and (3) causal validation via microglial depletion (PLX5622) and targeted BBB repair (Axitinib). In vitro, HT22 hippocampal neurons were stimulated with soluble inflammatory mediators released by primed microglia to assess direct synaptic injury.
RESULTS: MECT significantly impaired immediate and delayed associative memory and reduced left hippocampal ALFF in MDD patients; memory decline correlated with ALFF reduction. In a paired subgroup of patients, DCE-MRI revealed increased hippocampal Ktrans after MECT, providing preliminary clinical imaging support for treatment-associated BBB hyperpermeability. In CRS mice, ECS downregulated tight junction proteins (Claudin-5, ZO-1, Occludin), induced Evans blue extravasation, and promoted hippocampal deposition of fibrinogen and complement C3. ECS also triggered microglial activation, enhanced PSD95 synaptic phagocytosis, elevated IL-6/IL-1β, and reduced synaptic proteins. Critically, both PLX5622-mediated microglial depletion and Axitinib-mediated BBB repair reversed these pathological changes and rescued cognitive function, establishing a dual causal validation system. Axitinib failed to suppress LPS-induced microglial activation, suggesting its protective effects were mediated via BBB restoration rather than direct immunomodulation.
CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, this study identifies a hippocampus-centered neurovascular-immune mechanism underlying MECT/ECS-related cognitive impairment. Our findings demonstrate that BBB disruption is an early upstream event that permits peripheral factors to enter the brain, activate microglia, and drive synaptic injury and cognitive decline. These results establish a novel mechanistic framework for the cognitive side effects of MECT and highlight BBB protection and microglial modulation as potential strategies for cognitive protection.

A.title: Therapeutic strategies in vascular cognitive impairment: Insights from the bilateral common carotid artery stenosis mouse model.
A.abstract: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is a major consequence of cerebrovascular disease, but disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is increasingly recognized not simply as reduced cerebral blood flow, but as a sustained disturbance of oxygen delivery, capillary perfusion, neurovascular coupling, blood-brain barrier integrity, glial homeostasis, white matter maintenance, and synaptic network function. The bilateral common carotid artery stenosis (BCAS) mouse model is a central experimental platform for studying hypoperfusion-related VCI, as it exhibits reproducible cerebral blood flow reduction, white matter pathology, gliovascular injury, and cognitive impairment while permitting genetic manipulation, longitudinal imaging, retinal readouts, omics profiling, and therapeutic testing. This review synthesizes therapeutic studies in BCAS model mice across vascular/endothelial and hemodynamic mechanisms, oxidative and ferroptotic stress, ion-water transport, neuronal excitability and synaptic support, remote ischemic conditioning, regenerative and cell-based approaches, and biomarker-driven model refinement. Across these domains, successful interventions frequently converge on interconnected network nodes rather than isolated linear pathways, linking endothelial function, blood-brain barrier stability, redox-lipid balance, astrocytic ion-water regulation, microglial repair states, oligodendrocyte maturation, myelin integrity, and circuit plasticity. However, methodological heterogeneity concerning surgery, animal characteristics, behavioral testing, treatment timing, and outcome selection restricts translation. Future BCAS studies should prespecify treatment windows, particularly delayed-treatment paradigms initiated after objectively documented hypoperfusion, white matter injury, or cognitive impairment. Studies should also incorporate systemic dose-response assessments, biomarker-guided treatment stratification, clinically relevant comorbidities, and rational combination therapies. Such approaches may convert mechanistic insights from chronic hypoperfusion models into clinically credible therapeutic strategies for VCI.

A.title: Neuroprotective potential of vitamin D3 against glucocorticoid-induced neurotoxicity: Focus on calcium-binding proteins and neuroinflammation in a rat model.
A.abstract: Prolonged glucocorticoid (GC) therapy is frequently complicated by secondary vitamin D3 deficiency, which acts as a potential pathogenetic modulator of GC-induced neurotoxicity. This study investigated the role of disturbed calcium homeostasis and neuroinflammation in GC-induced brain damage and evaluated the protective potential of vitamin D3 (VD3, cholecalciferol). Female Wistar rats (n = 54) were divided into control, GC-treated (prednisolone, 5 mg/kg/day, 30 days, per os), and VD3-correction (1000 IU/kg/day, concurrent with GC) groups. Analysis of calcium-binding protein levels (calbindin-D28K, S100B, osteocalcin) and neurospecific markers (NF-L, MBP, GFAP) was performed using ELISA, Western blot, and confocal microscopy. Prolonged prednisolone administration caused significant systemic and local 25(OH)D3 deficiency, accompanied by a twofold reduction in osteocalcin protein content and elevated calbindin-D28K levels. Reactive astrogliosis, characterized by increased GFAP+ cell counts and S100B content, occurred alongside decline in NG2+ oligodendrocyte precursors. Significant neuroinflammation was recorded: TNF-α levels rose 1.62-fold in the cortex and 1.65-fold in the hippocampus, while IL-1β increased 2.66-fold and 2.40-fold, respectively. Furthermore, markedly increased serum levels of NF-L, S100B, GFAP, and MBP indicated alterations consistent with blood-brain barrier dysfunction and neuro-glial disintegration. VD3 therapy effectively restored serum markers (osteocalcin, S100B, MBP), suppressed astrocyte reactivity, and normalized cortical cytokine levels while partially replenishing NG2+ cell pool. Although its impact on hippocampal inflammation was limited, these findings demonstrate that maintaining adequate VD3 levels is paramount for preserving CNS integrity by stabilizing calcium buffering and suppressing neuroinflammation. Our results emphasize clinical importance of monitoring VD3 status to mitigate risk of glucocorticoid-induced neurotoxicity and associated neurological complications.

A.title: Structure-based discovery of acridone alkaloids as disruptors of the HEG1-KRIT1 protein-protein interaction in cerebral cavernous malformation signaling.
A.abstract: The HEG1-KRIT1 interaction is essential for endothelial cerebral cavernous malformation complex localization and signaling, making this interface a relevant target for chemical disruption. This study aimed to identify acridone alkaloids capable of inhibiting HEG1 binding to KRIT1 through integrated virtual screening, molecular simulations, binding-energy analysis, drug-likeness prediction, and experimental validation. Screening of 2,449 acridone alkaloids prioritized five candidates: 5-hydroxynoracronycine, acronycine, arborinine, glycocitrine I, and rutacridone. Computational analyses showed stable binding within the HEG1-recognition pocket of KRIT1 and predicted interface weakening, with rutacridone and 5-hydroxynoracronycine producing the strongest destabilizing effects. A bead-based flow-cytometry competition assay confirmed concentration-dependent inhibition, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration values of 2.21 ± 0.31 µM for rutacridone, 2.30 ± 0.30 µM for arborinine, and 2.90 ± 0.35 µM for 5-hydroxynoracronycine. These findings identify rutacridone, arborinine, and 5-hydroxynoracronycine as promising acridone-based starting points for developing HEG1-KRIT1 interaction disruptors. A.title: Giant mixed vascular lymphatic malformation in a pediatric patient: a case report.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Giant Mixed vascular lymphatic malformation-is a relatively rare congenital anomaly, particularly in pediatric populations. Mediastinal vascular malformations are uncommon in children, and their exact incidence remains poorly defined in the literature. It is not a true neoplasm but rather a low-flow vascular malformation arising from aberrant development of the vascular system during embryogenesis. Due to nonspecific clinical manifestations (e.g., cough, dyspnea) and the deep location of the mediastinum-adjacent to the heart, great vessels, and airways-diagnosis and management pose considerable challenges. Misdiagnosis is common, potentially leading to inappropriate treatment and life-threatening complications. Thus, accurate preoperative imaging is essential for developing safe and effective treatment strategies.
CASE DESCRIPTION: We report the case of a 3-year-old girl who presented with a persistent cough lasting more than 20 days. Imaging revealed a cystic-solid mass measuring approximately 53 mm × 37 mm × 67 mm in the left middle-upper mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed mild progressive enhancement of the lesion, with distinct "branch-like" vascular structures communicating with the left brachiocephalic vein, consistent with a low-flow vascular malformation. No definite arterial feeding vessel was identified. The mass was well-demarcated from the aorta and heart but caused localized compression and narrowing of the left main bronchus. These imaging findings were consistent with a low-flow vascular malformation. A biopsy obtained via video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) confirmed the diagnosis of mixed vascular malformation. Given the high-risk location adjacent to vital mediastinal structures, complete surgical resection was considered extremely hazardous. The multidisciplinary team therefore adopted a non-surgical approach consisting of oral sirolimus as targeted therapy. Following treatment, the child's cough improved significantly.
CONCLUSIONS: This case illustrates that in children with cystic-solid mediastinal masses, the presence of "progressive enhancement" and "clearly enhanced vascular channels" on contrast-enhanced CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should raise suspicion for vascular malformations. Comprehensive imaging assessment is fundamental for accurate diagnosis and formulation of individualized management. For complex mediastinal vascular malformations with high surgical risk, oral sirolimus represents a safe and effective targeted therapeutic alternative, capable of alleviating symptoms and controlling disease progression.

A.title: Current Therapeutic Options in Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
A.abstract: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a vascular malformation syndrome consisting of a facial port-wine birthmark associated with malformed leptomeningeal blood vessels and a choroid "angioma" of the eye. It is a rare neurocutaneous disorder that occurs sporadically, is not inherited, and is caused by a somatic mosaic mutation in GNAQ. In patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome, brain involvement typically presents in infancy with seizures, strokes, and stroke-like episodes, and a range of neurologic impairments. Standard treatment includes laser therapy for the birthmark, control of glaucoma through eyedrops or surgery, and the use of anticonvulsants. Increasingly low-dose aspirin is offered. Treatment with propranolol has been tried generally without the dramatic results seen in hemangiomas. Treatment with an anticonvulsant or low-dose aspirin or both before the onset of seizures is an option. Surgical resection may be offered to those whose seizures are medically refractory. Endocrine, medical rehabilitation and cognitive comorbidities are important to manage. In the future, new therapeutic options are likely to be offered stemming from preclinical studies and small pilot clinical trials currently ongoing. Discovery of the causative somatic mosaic mutation suggests new insights into the pathophysiology of this vascular malformation disorder, and potential novel treatment strategies for future study. The mutation results in constitutive overactivation of the Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK and the HIPPO-YAP pathways and inhibitors of these pathways may in the future prove useful in the treatment of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
